ann_37.text: Through this part, typical angina or non-anginal chest pain (about 22%) and atypical angina (about 28%) clearly lower a typical patient's predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms (about 59%).

Being a woman lowers it to about 6%, while going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises it to about 95%, higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 39% to about 81%, and higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 47% to about 72% (on the training data only).
A flat ST segment raises it to about 79% and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy to about 67% (on the training data only).
Through this part alone, a reversible defect on the thallium scan lowers it from about 59% to about 27% (on the training data only).

For two rare categories the model has little data on this: a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; about 16%) and a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 78%), both on the training data only.

ann_38.text: This part acts on 87 of 242 training patients (36%); 16 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 50-year-old man with atypical angina, a maximum heart rate of 171 beats per minute and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 11% to about 5% (on the training data only).

Through it, a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 32%, and only once the heart rate rises above about 167 beats per minute (on the training data only).

ann_39.text: This part acts on 103 of 242 training patients (43%); 19 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 47-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, a maximum heart rate of 163 beats per minute, a normal resting ECG and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 23% to about 3% (on the training data only).

Through it, older age (42 to 66 years) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 9% to about 63%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers it from about 59% to about 32% (on the training data only).
Older age clearly raises it here without a reversible thallium defect, but the other way with one (from about 9% to about 53%, against about 89% to about 31%).
A higher maximum heart rate clearly lowers it here, and even more so without a reversible thallium defect (from about 59% to about 32%, against about 67% to about 66% with one).
A higher maximum heart rate also clearly lowers it more for patients aged 56 or younger (from about 24% to about 10%, against about 63% to about 60% for older patients).

ann_40.text: This part acts on 108 of 242 training patients (45%), patients with a flat ST segment; 70 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 94% to about 98% (on the training data only).

Through it, a flat ST segment raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 74%, older age (42 to 66 years) from about 9% to about 63%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers it from about 59% to about 32% (on the training data only).
Higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) clearly raises it, and even more so with an upsloping ST segment (from about 39% to about 81%, against about 81% to about 94% with a flat one).
A reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it only slightly here, from about 59% to about 63%.

ann_41.text: This part acts on 92 of 242 training patients (38%); 70 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, chest pain brought on by exercise, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it clearly raises the predicted risk from about 92% to above 99%.
Through it, a reversible defect on the thallium scan clearly raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 86%.
Having any chest pain symptoms clearly lowers it here, and even more so with a reversible defect (from about 67% to about 12%, against about 59% to about 22% with a normal scan).
Older age (42 to 66 years) clearly raises it here without a reversible defect, but the other way with one (from about 9% to about 53%, against about 89% to about 31%).

A fixed thallium defect, age and chest pain type change that patient's predicted risk only slightly through this part (on the training data only; the model has little data on fixed defects, 15 patients).

ann_42.text: This part acts on 116 of 242 training patients (48%); 79 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it clearly raises the predicted risk from about 92% to above 99%.
Through it, a reversible defect on the thallium scan clearly raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 88%.
More ST depression on exercise clearly raises it here, and even more so with a reversible defect (from 0 to 2.8 mm, about 36% to about 99%, against about 59% to about 66% with a normal scan).
Typical angina clearly lowers it here, and even more so with a reversible defect (from about 67% to about 4%, against about 59% to about 11% with a normal scan).

Through this part, ST depression adds to the predicted risk only once it rises above about 1.4 mm (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 16% to about 51%), and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it only once it rises above about 167 beats per minute (from about 59% to about 25%) (on the training data only).

ann_43.text: This part acts on 84 of 242 training patients (35%); 46 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 64-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1 vessel coloured, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 99% to about 98% (on the training data only).
Through it, typical angina lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 40%, and older age (42 to 66 years) lowers it from about 59% to about 48% (on the training data only).
Age lowers the predicted risk through this part only once it rises above about 61 years (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 58% to about 42%) (on the training data only).
A downsloping ST segment lowers it here from about 59% to about 27% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 17 patients).
Higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) clearly raises it, and even more so for patients aged 56 or younger (from about 13% to about 49%, against about 44% to about 71% for older patients).

ann_44.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 11%), non-anginal chest pain (about 22%) or atypical angina (about 28%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 59%).

Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk to about 6%, going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises it to about 95%, and a flat ST segment raises it to about 88% (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) raises it from about 39% to about 81% and higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 47% to about 72%, while a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers it from about 59% to about 32% (on the training data only).
Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG raise it to about 67%, and more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) to about 66% (on the training data only).
The model ignores exercise-induced angina and fasting blood sugar.

ann_37.original: Supported. linear_score is a 12-input logistic-regression term (SD 2.31 logit on train, AUC 0.850 alone) led by ca +1.11, sex:0 -0.91 (sex:1 +0.55, so male +), cp:4 +0.81, chol +0.80, thal:7 -0.64, slope:2 +0.48, thal:6 -0.48, trestbps +0.42. The negative thal:7/thal:6 weights are counter-directional on their own but are more than offset by the nonlinear paths (thal:7 adds +1.34 via young_reserve being shut and +2.87 via st_defect_hinge on average). Evidence: sensitivity = |weights| (train, n=242): ca 1.11, sex:0 0.91, cp:4 0.81, chol 0.80, thal:7 0.64, sex:1 0.55, slope:2 0.48, thal:6 0.48, trestbps 0.42, slope:3 0.23, restecg:2 0.18, cp:2 0.14. Train: SD 2.31 logit, AUC 0.850 alone; replacing it by its mean drops full AUC 0.959 -> 0.875.
ann_37.proposed: An additive part: chest pain symptoms and being a woman lower the predicted risk; more vessels, higher cholesterol, higher resting blood pressure, a flat ST segment and left ventricular hypertrophy raise it; a reversible thallium defect lowers it here, against its effect in other parts.

ann_38.original: Supported. Three ReLU ramps on max heart rate: 5718 = ReLU(0.908 thalach - 0.10) (active 121/242) feeds young_reserve with weight 1.04; 7245 = ReLU(1.01 thalach - 1.53) (active 10) and 7595 = ReLU(0.994 thalach - 0.868) (active 49) read out -0.015 and -0.078: their joint logit contribution has SD 0.017 and is negligible (AUC unchanged at the mean). Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): 5718 0.45, 7595 0.20, 7245 0.04 per unit thalach. Active counts 121/49/10. Readout of 7245+7595 SD 0.017 logit; setting it to its mean leaves train AUC 0.9594.
ann_38.proposed: A maximum heart rate above about 167 beats per minute lowers the predicted risk through this part.

ann_39.original: Supported. 1718 = ReLU(-1.52 age - 1.14 thal:7 + 1.04 ReLU(0.91 thalach - 0.10) - 0.52) is a protective heart-rate-reserve gate: open for young patients without a reversible thallium defect who reach high max heart rate. Read out -1.13 (largest single nonlinear term after the hinge, SD 1.47 logit). Among non-thal:7 patients it is active for 60/60 youngest-tertile (mean 2.77, disease rate 0.10), 32/38 middle, 5/54 oldest; only 6/90 thal:7 patients. It drives the strong age effect for younger patients. 4256 = ReLU(-0.83*1718 - 1.06) is provably dead (pre-activation <= -1.06 since 1718 >= 0), so its +0.55 readout never contributes. Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): age 0.64, thal:7 0.48, thalach_ramp 0.44 on 1718; 4256 all 0 (never active). Corr(1718, age) -0.78, corr(1718, thalach) +0.51. Disease rate 0.18 when 1718 active (n=103) vs 0.63 inactive. Setting the 1718 readout to its mean drops train AUC 0.959 -> 0.933.
ann_39.proposed: A part that acts on 103 patients and lowers their predicted risk; through it a higher maximum heart rate lowers the risk, most for younger patients without a reversible thallium defect, and older age raises it.

ann_40.original: Supported. 1476 = ReLU(1.18 slope:2 + 0.07 slope:1 - 0.37 chol + 0.08 young_reserve - 0.03) is a flat-ST-slope indicator: active for 108/110 slope:2 patients (mean 1.22, range 0-2.24) and 0 for all others; within slope:2 it falls with cholesterol (corr -0.99). Read out +0.55 to the logit (on top of slope:2's +0.48 linear weight) and +0.09 into hinge 1946. The young_reserve input (0.08) is a weak serial coupling, the reason young_reserve sits under this annotation. The negative chol term partly cancels chol's +0.80 linear weight in flat-slope patients (clinically unmotivated; not interpreted). Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): slope:2 0.53, chol 0.16, young_reserve 0.04, slope:1 0.03. Active 108/110 slope:2, 0/132 others. Readout SD 0.37 logit; at its mean train AUC 0.959 -> 0.957.
ann_40.proposed: A part acting on patients with a flat ST segment that slightly raises their predicted risk; through it cholesterol raises the risk more with an upsloping ST segment.

ann_41.original: Supported. 3138 = ReLU(1.09 thal:7 + 0.11 thal:6 + 0.27 ReLU(0.995 thal:6 - 0.63) + 0.16 cp:4 - 0.31 age + 0.18) is a thallium-defect score: active for all 90 thal:7 patients (0.90-2.41, lower when older), all 15 thal:6 patients (0.12-1.25, boosted by the thal:6 flag 7354), and 2 others (<0.16). Its only live output feeds the hinge 1946 (weight 1.13). 3956 = ReLU(-0.88*3138 - 1.25) is provably dead (always 0), so its -0.69 readout never contributes. Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): thal:7 0.48, age 0.14, cp:4 0.07, thal:6 0.07 on 3138; 3956 identically 0. 3138 active 90/90 thal:7, 15/15 thal:6, 2/137 normal.
ann_41.proposed: A thallium-defect part acting on 92 patients: a reversible defect raises the predicted risk; with such a defect, chest pain symptoms lower it more and older age lowers it.

ann_42.original: Supported. 1946 = ReLU(1.13 thal_defect + 0.87 oldpeak + 0.41 sex:0 - 0.50 cp:1 + 0.09 flat_slope - 0.67) and 3284 = ReLU(1.61*1946 - 0.79), read out 0.64*1946 + 1.36*3284: a convex (two-kink) risk hinge in ST depression that is opened by a thallium defect. Mean contribution 3.09 logit for thal:7 patients vs 0.15 for normal-thal patients; among thal:7 it grows with oldpeak (0.40, 1.82, 3.36, 7.06 by oldpeak band; disease 0.44, 0.74, 0.84, 0.96). For normal-thal patients it opens only at high oldpeak (1.59 when oldpeak > 1 SD). Female sex raises it, typical angina (cp:1) lowers it. This is the largest nonlinear block (SD 2.43 logit). Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242), on 3284/1946: thal_defect 0.63/0.55, oldpeak 0.48/0.42, cp:1 0.27/0.24, sex:0 0.23/0.20, flat_slope 0.05/0.04. Corr(1946, oldpeak) 0.77. Combined readout SD 2.43; at its mean train AUC 0.959 -> 0.920.
ann_42.proposed: A part that acts on about half the patients and raises their predicted risk: a reversible thallium defect raises it, ST depression adds risk above about 1.4 mm and more so with a reversible defect, and typical angina lowers it.

ann_43.original: Supported. 3880 = ReLU(1.88 age + 0.76 cp:1 + 0.92 slope:3 + 0.96 ReLU(1.05 chol + 1.08) - 2.06), read out -0.60, lowers the logit for older patients: active for 1/81 youngest-tertile, 16/72 middle, 67/89 oldest (mean 1.52), more so with high cholesterol (3464 is an affine chol relay, active 213/242), typical angina or downsloping ST. Together with young_reserve it makes the age effect an inverted U: mean logit over train when age is set to -2, 0, +0.5, +1, +2 SD is -1.14, 0.59, 0.66, 0.35, -0.92. Clinically counter-directional (older patients with high cholesterol get less risk); the network may be correcting the linear chol weight and the hinge for older patients, but this is not established. Evidence: sensitivity (train, n=242): age 0.65, cp:1 0.26, chol 0.33, slope:3 0.32. Active 84/242. Corr(3880, age) 0.52, corr(3880, chol) 0.34. Readout SD 0.75; at its mean train AUC 0.959 -> 0.950.
ann_43.proposed: A part acting on 84 patients through which older age above about 61 years, typical angina and a downsloping ST segment lower the predicted risk.

ann_44.original: Supported. summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk of heart disease about 59%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk with typical angina (about 11%), non-anginal chest pain (about 22%) or atypical angina (about 28%).

Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk to about 6%, while going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises it to about 95%, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment to about 88%, and higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 39% to about 81% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect: going from 0 to 2.8 mm moves it from about 36% to about 99% with a reversible defect, and from about 59% to about 66% with a normal scan (or the undecoded code 4).

Older age (42 to 66 years) clearly raises the predicted risk if the thallium scan does not show a reversible defect, but the other way if it does: from about 9% to about 53% without one, and from about 89% to about 31% with one.

A maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 32%, and higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) raises it from about 47% to about 72% (on the training data only).
The model ignores exercise-induced angina and fasting blood sugar.
